action_criteria.expected_evidence: Active denervation in bulbar, cervical, thoracic and lumbosacral regions with chronic reinnervation in cervical and lumbosacral muscles; normal conduction velocities without conduction block; sensory studies normal apart from a mildly reduced right sural response.
action_criteria.label: EMG and nerve conduction studies of the bulbar, cervical, thoracic and lumbosacral regions to document lower motor neuron involvement and exclude conduction block and neuropathy
action_criteria.rationale: EMG/NCS confirms lower motor neuron involvement beyond the clinically affected muscles and excludes the main treatable mimics: multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block, demyelinating or sensorimotor neuropathy and myopathy. Gold Coast 2020 accepts EMG evidence of lower motor neuron dysfunction, and Awaji 2008 counts fasciculation potentials as active denervation in muscles with chronic neurogenic change.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Stable MS lesions with no new or enhancing lesion and no PML lesion; new symmetric precentral low T2 signal and corticospinal tract signal change separate from the known lesion (supportive only).
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI to exclude structural, vascular, demyelinating, inflammatory or neoplastic causes of the upper motor neuron or bulbar signs
action_criteria.rationale: MRI does not confirm ALS. It excludes brain and brainstem lesions that can cause upper motor neuron or bulbar signs, including MS activity and PML on natalizumab; corticospinal tract signal change, when present, is supportive only.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No demyelinating cord lesion, cord signal change or compression in the cervical or thoracic spine.
action_criteria.label: Spine MRI of the cervical and thoracic cord, and of the lumbosacral spine when lower limb signs need it, to exclude compressive myelopathy, radiculopathy and other cord lesions
action_criteria.rationale: Cervical spondylotic myelopathy with radiculopathy is the commonest structural mimic of combined upper and lower motor neuron signs in the limbs. Spine MRI excludes it, but incidental spondylosis does not explain bulbar signs or denervation in other regions and must not delay the ALS work-up.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: CK 498 U/L (2.9x ULN); blood count, renal and liver function, electrolytes, calcium, thyroid function, B12, folate, ESR and CRP normal.
action_criteria.label: Blood tests for treatable mimics and a pre-treatment baseline: full blood count, renal and liver function, electrolytes and calcium, CK, thyroid function, vitamin B12 and folate, ESR and CRP
action_criteria.rationale: These tests exclude metabolic, endocrine, nutritional and inflammatory mimics and give the liver and blood-count baseline needed before riluzole; phenotype-specific tests are added only when the case raises that mimic.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: WBC 3 cells/uL, protein 62 mg/dL, oligoclonal bands present (known MS), IgG index normal, JC virus PCR not detected.
action_criteria.label: CSF only for the specific mimic questions: oligoclonal bands and IgG index for MS activity, JC virus PCR for PML on natalizumab
action_criteria.rationale: CSF is not part of the routine ALS work-up and does not diagnose ALS. Here natalizumab with a positive JC virus antibody index raises a PML question, which the MRI largely answers, so CSF is optional.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: FVC 78% predicted (reduced) and SNIP 60 cmH2O (lower limit of normal for women): mild respiratory muscle weakness at baseline.
action_criteria.label: Baseline respiratory function (FVC and SNIP, with MIP where available) to stage respiratory muscle involvement and plan monitoring and NIV
action_criteria.rationale: Respiratory function does not diagnose ALS. Once ALS is supported it stages respiratory muscle weakness, sets the baseline for 3-monthly monitoring and identifies patients who need early referral for NIV.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No pathogenic C9orf72 expansion and no pathogenic variant in SOD1, TARDBP, FUS or TBK1; a negative result does not exclude ALS.
action_criteria.label: ALS gene panel (C9orf72 repeat expansion; SOD1, TARDBP, FUS and TBK1) after pre-test genetic counselling, once the clinical and electrodiagnostic assessment is complete
action_criteria.rationale: Genetic testing does not make the diagnosis. It is offered with counselling to people with ALS because a pathogenic variant changes counselling for relatives and may open gene-targeted treatment or trials.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No pharmacokinetic interaction with natalizumab, escitalopram, lisinopril or vitamin D; transaminase monitoring covers the rare natalizumab liver injury; natalizumab lymphocytosis affects the white cell count.
action_criteria.label: Check riluzole against the current medicines, alcohol use and liver function before the first dose, once the diagnosis is established
action_criteria.rationale: Riluzole is metabolised by CYP1A2 and can raise liver transaminases, so the medicine list, alcohol use and baseline liver function are reviewed before treatment. Natalizumab does not interact with it, but both can rarely affect the liver, so one LFT schedule serves both.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not treat ALS with corticosteroids, IVIG or plasma exchange: they have no benefit.
Do not wait for FVC to fall below 50% or for respiratory symptoms before referring for NIV assessment.
Do not treat the new tongue wasting, fasciculations and multi-region denervation as an MS relapse with corticosteroids.
Do not attribute the progressive weakness, wasting or bulbar signs to depression or a functional disorder.
required_recommendations: Make and explain the diagnosis of ALS by Gold Coast 2020 criteria: progressive bilateral upper limb weakness with upper motor neuron signs (a brisk jaw jerk, new bilateral Hoffman signs and a new left extensor plantar response) and lower motor neuron involvement in the bulbar, cervical and lumbosacral regions on examination and EMG, with active denervation also in thoracic paraspinal muscles, with mimics excluded by MRI and blood tests; disclose it in a planned face-to-face discussion with the patient and family.

Refer to the respiratory/NIV service now because FVC is already reduced (78% predicted) and SNIP is at the lower limit of normal (60 cmH2O); screen for orthopnoea and nocturnal hypoventilation with overnight oximetry or capnography, and repeat FVC and SNIP within 3 months.
Arrange a speech and language therapy assessment of speech and swallowing, with communication support, and monitor weight and swallowing at each review.

Offer riluzole 50 mg twice daily. Measure liver transaminases before the first dose, monthly for 3 months, every 3 months for the rest of the first year and periodically thereafter; stop riluzole if ALT exceeds 5x the upper limit of normal, and ask the patient to report any febrile illness so that neutropenia can be excluded.

Refer to a specialist ALS multidisciplinary team (neurologist, specialist nurse, respiratory, speech and language therapy, dietetics, physiotherapy, occupational therapy and palliative care), reviewed about every 2 to 3 months, with an early, patient-paced discussion of advance care planning.
Offer genetic counselling and, if the patient wishes, ALS genetic testing, explaining the implications for relatives.
Inform the MS team; decisions on continuing natalizumab (JC virus antibody positive) stay with them.

avoided_actions.rationale: ALS is a motor-neuron disease without cortical electrical signature; EEG has no diagnostic role and adds cost without benefit.
ECG is unrelated to motor neuron disease and not part of the standard ALS workup absent specific cardiac symptoms or pre-medication QTc checks.
Echocardiography is unrelated to ALS diagnosis; no indication absent comorbid cardiac disease.
Cardiac monitoring has no role in ALS diagnostic workup.
MRI is the standard structural study for ALS workup; head CT adds no diagnostic value and exposes the patient to ionizing radiation.
Amyloid PET has no role in ALS diagnosis (motor-neuron rather than amyloid pathology) and carries a high cost.
DaTscan evaluates nigrostriatal dopaminergic integrity; it has no role in ALS, which spares the dopaminergic system.
FDG-PET has no established diagnostic role in ALS and adds substantial cost.

accepted: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) concurrent with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis

differential.key_features: supports: known RRMS with baseline right leg spasticity and right-sided sensory symptoms; against: MS does not cause tongue atrophy, fasciculations, wasting or EMG denervation, and the brain MRI shows no new or enhancing lesion
supports: natalizumab with a positive JC virus antibody index; against: no PML lesion on MRI, CSF JC virus PCR not detected, and PML does not produce lower motor neuron denervation

against: normal motor conduction velocities and distal latencies, no conduction block or temporal dispersion
against: tongue atrophy, wasting and EMG denervation are organic findings

key_clinical_evidence: Gold Coast 2020: ALS needs progressive motor impairment with upper and lower motor neuron dysfunction in at least one body region, or lower motor neuron dysfunction in at least two, after other diseases are excluded. Here: a brisk jaw jerk, new bilateral Hoffman signs and a new left extensor plantar response with lower motor neuron involvement in the bulbar, cervical and lumbosacral regions, with active denervation also in thoracic paraspinal muscles.
EMG lower motor neuron evidence is chronic neurogenic change with active denervation; by Awaji 2008 fasciculation potentials count as active denervation in a muscle with chronic neurogenic change.

A mildly reduced right sural response is a minor, non-specific sensory finding and does not explain widespread motor denervation; motor conduction is normal with no conduction block, which argues against multifocal motor neuropathy.
CK 498 U/L (2.9x ULN): mild to moderate elevation is common in ALS from denervation and does not by itself suggest a myopathy.

FVC 78% predicted is reduced and SNIP 60 cmH2O is at the lower limit of normal for women. AAN 2009 markers that prompt NIV discussion are orthopnoea, FVC below 50% predicted, SNIP below 40 cmH2O, MIP weaker than -60 cmH2O or abnormal overnight oximetry; NIV prolongs survival and improves quality of life (Bourke 2006).

Multiple sclerosis does not explain lower motor neuron signs in several regions: new tongue atrophy and fasciculations, wasting and multi-region EMG denervation indicate a second process, while the stable MRI without new or enhancing lesions argues against MS activity. Upper motor neuron signs are harder to attribute in MS, so the new bilateral Hoffman signs and new left extensor plantar response are judged against the earlier examination.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: MS is a confounder, not the explanation: stable MS lesions explain her baseline right leg spasticity and right-sided sensory symptoms, but not tongue atrophy and fasciculations, new muscle wasting, widespread fasciculations or multi-region lower motor neuron denervation on EMG; the brain MRI shows no new or enhancing lesion.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchors weakness on MS relapse or progression

sequence_constraints.reason: Genetic testing follows the clinical and electrodiagnostic assessment and pre-test counselling; it does not make the diagnosis.

patient.history_present_illness:
Ms. W is a 63-year-old woman with an 18-year history of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis on natalizumab who presents with 8-month progressive arm weakness, tongue wasting, and new fasciculations that she and her neurologist agree represent symptoms beyond what is expected from her MS baseline.

Her MS has been well-controlled on natalizumab with no relapses in 6 years. Her last MRI 14 months ago showed no new lesions, stable white matter disease burden, and a chronic left corticospinal tract lesion explaining her longstanding right leg spasticity. On review of her recent examination, her neurologist was alarmed by several new features: bilateral tongue atrophy and fasciculations (not present on examination 2 years ago), new bilateral arm weakness with muscle wasting including thenar atrophy, and new visible muscle twitching in her arms and calves.

She describes 8 months of progressive bilateral arm and hand weakness that does not follow the pattern of her prior MS relapses (which were typically unilateral, sudden onset, partially reversible). The current progression is insidious and continuous. She has noticed wasting of her hand muscles and has had difficulty with fine motor tasks. She has also noticed new tongue twitching and mild difficulty articulating clearly.

Her MS neurologist is concerned that she may have developed a new, second neurological process with lower motor neuron features distinct from her MS. Her JC virus antibody index is elevated and is monitored because of the PML risk on natalizumab.
